title: How to Find a Real Estate Investing Coach (And Actually Get Your Money's Worth)
excerpt: Finding the right real estate investing coach can cut years off your learning curve and help you close deals faster. Here's a step-by-step guide to identifying, vetting, and working with a coach who delivers real results.
author: AIWholesail Team
tags: how to find a real estate investing coach
metaDescription: Learn how to find a real estate investing coach who fits your goals, budget, and strategy. Includes vetting tips, red flags, and cost breakdowns.
metaKeywords: how to find a real estate investing coach, real estate coaching, real estate mentor, real estate investing coach, wholesale real estate coach, real estate coach cost, real estate mentorship

sections.content: Every successful real estate investor has a story about the moment things clicked. For a lot of them, that moment came when they started working with a coach or mentor. A good coach helps you avoid costly mistakes, holds you accountable, and gives you a proven playbook to follow. But finding the right one? That takes some work. This guide will walk you through exactly how to find a real estate investing coach who is worth your time and money.
Why a Real Estate Investing Coach Is Worth Considering

Real estate investing has a steep learning curve. You have to understand deal analysis, negotiation, financing, market trends, and exit strategies all at once. If you are just getting started, check out our [Real Estate Investing for Beginners guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/real-estate-investing-for-beginners) to build a solid foundation before hiring a coach. That said, a coach accelerates your growth in ways that books and YouTube videos simply cannot. Studies from the International Coaching Federation show that people who work with coaches see an average ROI of 7x their investment. In real estate, where a single deal can generate $10,000 to $50,000 or more in profit, the math makes a lot of sense.
Step 1: Get Clear on What You Need Before You Search

Before you start searching for a coach, you need to know what you are trying to accomplish. Are you brand new and looking to close your first wholesale deal? Are you a landlord trying to scale from 5 units to 50? Are you a house flipper who needs help running the numbers? Your strategy determines the type of coach you need. A wholesaling expert may not be the best fit if your goal is building a rental portfolio, and vice versa.

items: Define your investing strategy: wholesaling, flipping, buy-and-hold, BRRRR, etc.
Set a clear goal: first deal in 90 days, $5,000/month cash flow, 10 flips per year
Decide on your budget for coaching: most programs range from $2,000 to $25,000+
Determine how much time you can commit to coaching calls and assignments each week
Identify your biggest gaps: deal finding, analyzing deals, financing, negotiation, or systems

sections.content: Step 2: Know Where to Look for Qualified Coaches

Real estate investing coaches are everywhere online, which makes it both easy and risky to find one. The best coaches are often found through warm referrals rather than paid ads. Ask your local real estate investment association (REIA) for recommendations. Check BiggerPockets forums, where active investors frequently discuss coaches they have worked with. Local investor meetups in active markets like [Atlanta](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga), [Dallas](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx), and [Phoenix](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az) are also great places to meet coaches face to face and get a feel for their teaching style before committing any money.
Places to Find Real Estate Investing Coaches

items: Local REIA meetings and national real estate conferences
BiggerPockets forums and the BiggerPockets Pro network
LinkedIn searches for active real estate investors who also coach
Referrals from other investors in your market
YouTube and podcast channels where coaches demonstrate their knowledge for free
Real estate masterminds and group programs
Online coaching directories like Coach.me or Clarity.fm

sections.content: Before paying for any coaching program, consume at least 5 to 10 hours of free content from that coach. Their YouTube videos, podcast episodes, or blog posts will tell you a lot about the quality of their knowledge and whether their teaching style works for you.
Step 3: Vet Every Coach Thoroughly

This is where most beginners skip ahead too quickly. The real estate coaching industry has no licensing requirements, which means anyone can call themselves a coach. Vetting thoroughly is non-negotiable. You want to see proof that your potential coach is actively investing in real estate today, not just someone who did a few deals in 2012 and now sells courses. Ask for recent transaction history, references from current students, and specific examples of deals they have closed in the last 12 months.
Questions to Ask Before Hiring a Real Estate Coach

items: How many deals have you closed in the past 12 months and in what markets?
Can you provide three references from students who have closed deals with your guidance?
What does your coaching program include and how often do we meet?
Do you have experience in my specific investing strategy and target market?
What happens if I am not getting results after 60 or 90 days?
Is there a contract and what is the refund policy?
Do you also invest your own money in deals, or is coaching your primary income?

sections.content: Step 4: Watch for Red Flags

Not every coach has your best interests in mind. Some are primarily focused on selling you into expensive programs with little ongoing support. A big red flag is any coach who guarantees specific profits or claims you will make six figures in your first year with no experience. Another warning sign is a coach who can only show you testimonials but cannot provide actual student references you can call. Be especially cautious of programs that pressure you to sign up immediately with a limited-time discount. Legitimate coaches are confident enough in their value that they do not need high-pressure sales tactics.

The best mentors don't just give you fish — they teach you how to analyze the pond, pick the right bait, and build systems so you never go hungry. If your coach can't explain their own deal-finding process in detail, they probably can't teach it to you either.
Step 5: Understand What Real Coaching Costs

Real estate coaching costs vary widely based on the coach's experience, the depth of the program, and the level of one-on-one access you receive. Entry-level group programs often range from $2,000 to $5,000. Mid-tier programs with more personal access typically cost $5,000 to $15,000. High-end one-on-one mentorship can run $15,000 to $50,000 or more. Be realistic about what you are getting at each price point. A $2,000 group program will not give you the same personalized attention as a $12,000 one-on-one coaching engagement. That said, some of the most valuable mentorship in real estate is completely free — it comes from experienced investors who are willing to partner on deals in exchange for your time and effort.
Free and Low-Cost Alternatives to Paid Coaching

items: Find a deal-based mentor who takes a small percentage of your first few deals in exchange for guidance
Join a local REIA and volunteer to help experienced investors with tasks in exchange for knowledge
Partner with an active investor on your first deal as a way to learn and earn simultaneously
Use free online resources like BiggerPockets, YouTube channels, and forums to build foundational knowledge
Attend free or low-cost real estate bootcamps and masterminds in your area

sections.content: Step 6: Get the Tools to Back Up What You Learn

Even the best coaching is only as effective as the tools you use to execute. Once your coach teaches you how to evaluate deals, you need reliable software to run the numbers quickly and accurately. Whether you are wholesaling properties or flipping houses, use the free [Wholesale Deal Calculator at AIWholesail](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/wholesale-deal-calculator) to analyze your first deals and make sure your offers are profitable. If your coach is focused on wholesaling, also check out the [Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesaling-real-estate-for-beginners) to understand the mechanics behind each step your coach is teaching you.

Track every deal you analyze during your coaching program in a simple spreadsheet. After 30 days, review what you analyzed versus what you offered on versus what you actually closed. This data will help you and your coach identify exactly where deals are slipping through the cracks.
What Good Coaching Actually Looks Like in Practice

A solid coaching engagement typically includes weekly or bi-weekly calls, deal reviews where your coach looks at real deals you are analyzing, accountability check-ins, access to a community of other students, and clear milestones. For example, a wholesaling coach might set a 30-day goal of making 50 motivated seller calls, a 60-day goal of submitting your first offer, and a 90-day goal of closing your first deal. Good coaches make the path concrete and measurable, not vague and inspirational.
